findings.summary: Four-GPU embedding reduced NACA embedding to 0.119 s. OCR now accounts for 89.2% of call time; embedding is 5.1% and rendering 4.9%.
observations: Three ordinary diagnostic calls had a 2.364 s median. The additional instrumented call passed exact OCR/chunk and frozen-vector checks.
Every measured call distributed 25 chunks over four embedding replicas: 6/7/5/7 chunks and 1,725/1,718/1,713/1,738 current input tokens. Outputs were restored to source order.
Each GPU recorded 2,336 small decoder matrix launches across 32 instrumented steps, confirming that retained fixed 32-row tiles remained active.
Seven one-second samples per GPU showed mean busy levels of 75.6%, 85.4%, 67.0% and 69.4%. These are activity samples, not proof of peak compute or bandwidth saturation.
vLLM waiting requests stayed at zero in sampled telemetry. NACA draft acceptance was only 1.8–2.9%; earlier full-dataset tests of two/eight proposals did not improve on four.
Full evaluation improved p50 speedup 7.0%, p95 3.4% and throughput 3.9% versus the fresh single-GPU embedding control. All 60 calls passed, but compilation raised candidate suite runtime to 450 s.
findings.next_step: Retain four-GPU embedding. Bitmap-format tuning was flat. Separate rendering processes helped NACA and Attention but regressed simpler PDFs; test rendering inside the existing OCR page workers to avoid image transfers through the parent.
findings.optimization: Optional page-worker rendering with exact pixel and frozen-output checks. Keep parent rendering as the fresh control and report overlapping render/OCR wall time honestly.
